Wassily Kandinsky, the Russian painter and theorist who pioneered abstract art—the radical notion that painting need not represent the visual world.

Born in Moscow, he trained as a lawyer before studying art in his late twenties, an unusually late start. In 1911, he co-founded Der Blaue Reiter, The Blue Rider, in Munich—one of Expressionism's most important groups. Around 1910, he created what many consider the first abstract paintings, non-representational compositions of pure color, line, and form.

Kandinsky developed a systematic color theory that assigned emotional associations to hues. Yellow is aggressive. Blue is spiritual. Black is silent. Red is energetic and sunny. His conviction that color and form possessed intrinsic emotional and musical qualities led him to create some of the first entirely non-objective paintings. He believed abstract art could express universal spiritual truths that representational art could never achieve.

When he taught at the Bauhaus in Weimar and Dessau during the nineteen twenties, he influenced generations of design and painting students. His influential treatise Concerning the Spiritual in Art, published in nineteen eleven, established abstraction as a philosophical movement, not merely a style. The work remains a foundational text in art theory, arguing that color and form possess inherent emotional resonance.

In nineteen thirty-three, he fled Nazi Germany and spent his final years in Paris, continuing to paint abstract works. His late paintings grew increasingly geometric and controlled, incorporating mathematical principles while maintaining their spiritual aspiration. He bridged Russian avant-garde and German modernism, influencing both Constructivist ideology and Bauhaus pedagogy across two continents.
